docs.title: About BitVMX
docs.text:
BitVMX is an open-source framework that enables blockchains and rollups to use Bitcoin as their settlement and dispute layer for critical operations such as withdrawals and bridge transfers.

Built on the BitVM family of ideas, BitVMX turns research into a complete, practical implementation: a deterministic virtual machine, a dispute engine, a transaction graph on Bitcoin, off-chain coordinators, signer and watcher clients, and full integration tooling.

With BitVMX, any chain can route verifiable claims—such as a withdrawal proof or bridge state update—through Bitcoin itself. When operators disagree, Bitcoin becomes the final arbiter of correctness under a simple 1-of-N honest operator assumption, eliminating the need for custodial multisigs, committees, or governance keys.

BitVMX is chain-agnostic by design. It integrates with any execution environment without requiring teams to build their own circuit compilers, dispute models, or Bitcoin transaction choreography. It already powers early cross-chain efforts, including the Bitcoin–Cardano Cardinal bridge and the Bitcoin–Rootstock Union bridge.

BitVMX exists to make Bitcoin-anchored settlement a real-world system you can actually deploy.

docs.title: Broker API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Broker service.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitvmx_broker Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Broker (bitvmx_broker) is a message broker service that handles identity, routing, and message transport between operators in the BitVMX network.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• TLS Authentication: Certificate validation via public key hash
  • Message Routing: Configurable routing tables and allowlists
  • Dual-Channel API: Bidirectional communication support
  • Coordination: Internal sub-component and cross-operator messaging

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-broker = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitvmx_broker::{BrokerClient, BrokerConfig};

// Initialize broker client
let config = BrokerConfig::from_file("config.yaml")?;
let client = BrokerClient::new(config)?;

// Send a message
client.send("peer_id", message_bytes)?;

// Receive messages
let message = client.receive()?;

docs.title: Configuring Routing
docs.text:
# config.yaml
allowlist:
  - peer_id: "abc123"
    address: "10.0.0.1"

routing_table:
  - source: "peer1"
    destination: "peer2"

docs.title: Message Handling
docs.text:
// Subscribe to messages
client.subscribe("topic", |msg| {
    println!("Received: {:?}", msg);
})?;

docs.title: Client API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Client library.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitvmx_client Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Client (bitvmx_client) is the main entry point for interacting with BitVMX protocols and the Bitcoin blockchain. It provides a comprehensive CLI and programmatic interface for protocol execution, transaction management, and Bitcoin integration.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Protocol Execution: Run BitVMX protocols (Cardinal, Union, etc.)
  • JSON RPC API: Message-based communication over BitVMX broker
  • Transaction Management: Dispatch, track, and verify Bitcoin transactions
  • Key Management: Integrated cryptographic operations
  • SPV Proof Generation: Create and verify SPV proofs

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-client = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-client.git", branch = "v.0.0.2" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitvmx_client::Client;

// Create a new client
let client = Client::new(config)?;

// Initialize a protocol
client.setup_protocol(protocol_config)?;

// Execute protocol steps
client.execute()?;

docs.title: Running Union Bridge Protocols
docs.text:
// Set up Union Bridge protocol
let protocol = client.setup_union_protocol(
    funding_tx,
    operator_keys,
)?;

// Execute peg-in flow
client.execute_pegin(protocol)?;

docs.title: Transaction Operations
docs.text:
// Dispatch a transaction
let txid = client.dispatch_transaction(tx)?;

// Query transaction status
let status = client.get_transaction_status(txid)?;

// Generate SPV proof
let proof = client.generate_spv_proof(txid)?;

docs.title: Key Management Integration
docs.text:
// Generate keys
let keypair = client.generate_keypair()?;

// Sign with MuSig2
let signature = client.musig2_sign(message, keypairs)?;

docs.title: API Messages
docs.text:
The client communicates via JSON RPC messages over the BitVMX broker. See API Messages for details on:

  • Program Management (Setup, Store Variables, Witness Data)
  • Transaction Management (Queries, Dispatching, SPV Proofs)
  • Subscriptions (Transaction updates, UTXO spending, RSK pegin)
  • Wallet Operations (Balance, Addresses, Fund transfers)
  • Key Management (Generation, Aggregation, Signing)
  • Zero-Knowledge Proofs (Generation, Result retrieval)

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
The BitVMX client also provides a CLI:

# Run a protocol
bitvmx-client run --protocol union --config config.yaml

# Query status
bitvmx-client status --txid <txid>

# Generate keys
bitvmx-client keygen --output keys.json

docs.text:
High-level guide for using the Bitcoin Coordinator.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitcoin_coordinator Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Bitcoin Coordinator (bitcoin_coordinator) is the central orchestration system for Bitcoin transaction management, dispatching, confirmation tracking, and applying fee speedups (CPFP/RBF) when needed.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Transaction Dispatch: Submit and track Bitcoin transactions
  • Confirmation Monitoring: Track transaction confirmations
  • Fee Management: Automatic CPFP and RBF speedups
  • Persistent State: Maintains state across restarts

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitcoin-coordinator = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitcoin_coordinator::Coordinator;

// Initialize coordinator
let coordinator = Coordinator::new(config)?;

// Dispatch a transaction
let txid = coordinator.dispatch_tx(transaction)?;

// Track confirmations
let confirmations = coordinator.get_confirmations(txid)?;

docs.title: Transaction Monitoring
docs.text:
// Monitor transaction until confirmed
coordinator.wait_for_confirmations(txid, 6).await?;

// Check if transaction needs speedup
if coordinator.needs_speedup(txid)? {
    coordinator.apply_rbf(txid)?;
}

docs.title: Batch Operations
docs.text:
// Dispatch multiple transactions
let txids = coordinator.dispatch_batch(transactions)?;

// Monitor batch completion
coordinator.wait_for_batch(txids, 6).await?;

docs.title: Indexer API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the Bitcoin Indexer.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitcoin_indexer Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Bitcoin Indexer (bitcoin_indexer) is a fast, persistent blockchain indexing solution that connects to Bitcoin Core and stores block and transaction IDs into RocksDB for efficient historical access.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Fast Indexing: Deterministic, block-by-block processing
  • Persistent Storage: RocksDB-based storage for quick lookups
  • Configurable Start Height: Partial syncs from specific block heights
  • Efficient Queries: Quick access to historical blockchain data

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitcoin-indexer = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitcoin_indexer::Indexer;

// Initialize indexer
let indexer = Indexer::new(config)?;

// Start indexing from a specific height
indexer.sync_from_height(700000)?;

// Query indexed data
let tx = indexer.get_transaction(txid)?;
let block = indexer.get_block(block_hash)?;

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
// Sync to tip of blockchain
indexer.sync_to_tip()?;

// Get current sync status
let status = indexer.sync_status()?;
println!("Height: {}, Synced: {}", status.height, status.is_synced);

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
// Get transaction by ID
let tx = indexer.get_tx_by_id(txid)?;

// Get block by height
let block = indexer.get_block_at_height(750000)?;

// Check if transaction exists
if indexer.has_tx(txid)? {
    println!("Transaction found");
}

docs.title: Key Manager API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Key Manager.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the key_manager Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Key Manager (key_manager) is a Rust library for cryptographic key management supporting multiple signature schemes including ECDSA, Schnorr, Winternitz one-time signatures, and MuSig2.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Multiple Signature Schemes: ECDSA, Schnorr, Winternitz OTS, MuSig2
  • Secure Storage: Keys are encrypted and persisted via Storage Backend
  • Hierarchical Key Derivation: BIP32/BIP44 support
  • Taproot Support: Full support for Taproot tweaks (key and script paths)
  • Key Import/Export: Flexible key management workflows

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-key-manager = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use key_manager::KeyManager;

// Initialize key manager
let key_manager = KeyManager::new(storage)?;

// Generate a new key
let keypair = key_manager.generate_keypair()?;

// Store the key
key_manager.store_key("my_key", keypair)?;

// Load a key
let loaded_key = key_manager.load_key("my_key")?;

docs.title: ECDSA Signing
docs.text:
// Generate ECDSA key
let ecdsa_key = key_manager.generate_ecdsa()?;

// Sign a message
let signature = key_manager.sign_ecdsa(message, &ecdsa_key)?;

// Verify signature
let valid = key_manager.verify_ecdsa(message, &signature, &ecdsa_key.public)?;

docs.title: Schnorr Signatures
docs.text:
// Generate Schnorr key
let schnorr_key = key_manager.generate_schnorr()?;

// Sign with Schnorr
let signature = key_manager.sign_schnorr(message, &schnorr_key)?;

// Verify
let valid = key_manager.verify_schnorr(message, &signature, &schnorr_key.public)?;

docs.title: MuSig2 (Multi-Party Signatures)
docs.text:
// Generate keys for multiple parties
let key1 = key_manager.generate_schnorr()?;
let key2 = key_manager.generate_schnorr()?;

// Aggregate public keys
let agg_key = key_manager.musig2_aggregate_keys(vec![&key1.public, &key2.public])?;

// Create nonces
let nonce1 = key_manager.musig2_nonce_gen(&key1)?;
let nonce2 = key_manager.musig2_nonce_gen(&key2)?;

// Sign (each party)
let partial_sig1 = key_manager.musig2_partial_sign(message, &key1, &nonce1, vec![&nonce2])?;
let partial_sig2 = key_manager.musig2_partial_sign(message, &key2, &nonce2, vec![&nonce1])?;

// Aggregate signatures
let final_sig = key_manager.musig2_aggregate_signatures(vec![&partial_sig1, &partial_sig2])?;

docs.title: Winternitz One-Time Signatures
docs.text:
// Generate Winternitz keypair
let wots_key = key_manager.generate_winternitz()?;

// Sign (can only sign once!)
let wots_signature = key_manager.sign_winternitz(message, &wots_key)?;

// Verify
let valid = key_manager.verify_winternitz(message, &wots_signature, &wots_key.public)?;

docs.title: Taproot Support
docs.text:
// Generate Taproot key
let internal_key = key_manager.generate_schnorr()?;

// Apply script path tweak
let script_tree = /* build script tree */;
let tweaked_key = key_manager.taproot_tweak_key(&internal_key, script_tree)?;

// Sign with tweaked key (key path spend)
let signature = key_manager.sign_taproot_keypath(message, &tweaked_key)?;

docs.title: Key Storage
docs.text:
Keys are automatically encrypted and stored via the Storage Backend:

// Store a key with a name
key_manager.store_key("operator_key", keypair)?;

// List all stored keys
let keys = key_manager.list_keys()?;

// Delete a key
key_manager.delete_key("old_key")?;

docs.title: Protocol Builder API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Protocol Builder.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the protocol_builder Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Protocol Builder (protocol_builder) is a Rust library for designing Bitcoin protocols as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of pre-signed transactions, enabling complex multi-step Bitcoin interactions.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• DAG-Based Design: Model protocols as graphs where transactions are nodes and spends are edges
  • Multi-Signature Support: ECDSA, Schnorr, MuSig2, Winternitz one-time signatures
  • Automatic Fee Management: Estimate sizes and apply fee margins automatically
  • Visualization: Export protocols as Graphviz diagrams for auditing
  • CPFP Support: Child-Pays-For-Parent for handling congestion

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-protocol-builder = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use protocol_builder::ProtocolBuilder;

// Create a new protocol builder
let mut builder = ProtocolBuilder::new();

// Add transactions to the protocol
let funding_tx = builder.add_transaction("funding", funding_tx_data)?;
let setup_tx = builder.add_transaction("setup", setup_tx_data)?;

// Link transactions (spending relationships)
builder.link(funding_tx, setup_tx, 0)?; // spend output 0 of funding in setup

// Build the protocol
let protocol = builder.build()?;

docs.title: Building a Payment Channel
docs.text:
// Create protocol
let mut protocol = ProtocolBuilder::new();

// Add funding transaction
let funding = protocol.add_external_utxo(outpoint)?;

// Add setup transaction (establishes channel)
let setup = protocol.add_transaction("setup")
    .add_input_from(funding, 0)?
    .add_taproot_output(channel_script, amount)?
    .build()?;

// Add commitment transactions
let commitment_a = protocol.add_transaction("commit_a")
    .add_input_from(setup, 0)?
    .add_output(alice_address, alice_amount)?
    .add_output(bob_address, bob_amount)?
    .build()?;

// Sign and finalize
protocol.sign_with_musig2(operator_keys)?;
let final_protocol = protocol.finalize()?;

docs.title: Automatic Fee Management
docs.text:
// Use AUTO_AMOUNT for automatic fee calculation
let tx = protocol.add_transaction("payment")
    .add_input_from(prev_tx, 0)?
    .add_output(recipient, AUTO_AMOUNT)? // Automatically deducts fees
    .with_fee_rate(10)? // 10 sat/vB
    .build()?;

docs.title: Visualizing Protocols
docs.text:
// Export protocol as Graphviz DOT
let dot = protocol.to_graphviz()?;
std::fs::write("protocol.dot", dot)?;

// Render with: dot -Tpng protocol.dot -o protocol.png

docs.title: Transaction Types
docs.text:
The builder supports various transaction types:

  • SegWit (P2WPKH): Traditional segregated witness
  • Taproot (P2TR): Key path and script path spending
  • MuSig2: Aggregated signatures for multiple parties
  • Winternitz OTS: One-time signatures for BitVMX challenge-response

docs.title: Settings API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Settings library.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitvmx_settings Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Settings (bitvmx_settings) is a lightweight configuration management tool that loads configurations based on environment awareness and provides standardized runtime settings across BitVMX services.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Environment Awareness: Loads configurations based on BITVMX_ENV variable
  • YAML Format: Human-readable configuration files
  • CLI Overrides: Override settings via command-line flags
  • Validation: Type-safe configuration with validation

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-settings = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitvmx_settings::Settings;

// Load settings (uses BITVMX_ENV to determine environment)
let settings = Settings::load()?;

// Access configuration values
let bitcoin_rpc_url = settings.bitcoin.rpc_url;
let network = settings.network;

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
# config/development.yaml
network: regtest
bitcoin:
  rpc_url: "http://localhost:18443"
  rpc_user: "user"
  rpc_password: "password"
storage:
  path: "/tmp/bitvmx"

docs.title: Environment-Specific Configs
docs.text:
# Load development config
export BITVMX_ENV=development
cargo run

# Load production config
export BITVMX_ENV=production
cargo run

docs.title: CLI Overrides
docs.text:
use bitvmx_settings::Settings;

// Override from CLI
let settings = Settings::load_with_overrides(vec![
    "--configuration", "custom.yaml",
    "-c", "other.yaml"
])?;

docs.title: Configuration Structure
docs.text:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
pub struct Settings {
    pub network: Network,
    pub bitcoin: BitcoinConfig,
    pub storage: StorageConfig,
    pub logging: LoggingConfig,
    // ... other settings
}

docs.title: Storage Backend API
docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Storage Backend library.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the storage_backend Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Storage Backend (storage_backend) is a RocksDB-based encrypted storage solution that provides transactional key-value storage for persisting BitVMX state across the entire stack.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Encrypted Storage: All data is encrypted at rest
  • Transaction Support: Full ACID compliance with begin, commit, and rollback operations
  • Prefix Queries: Efficiently filter by key prefixes for indexing and metadata
  • High Performance: Built on RocksDB for fast, persistent storage

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
rust-bitvmx-storage-backend = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use storage_backend::StorageBackend;

// Initialize storage
let storage = StorageBackend::new("/path/to/db")?;

// Write data
storage.put(b"key", b"value")?;

// Read data
let value = storage.get(b"key")?;

// Delete data
storage.delete(b"key")?;

docs.title: Working with Transactions
docs.text:
// Begin a transaction
let txn = storage.begin()?;

// Perform multiple operations
txn.put(b"key1", b"value1")?;
txn.put(b"key2", b"value2")?;

// Commit the transaction
txn.commit()?;

docs.title: Prefix Queries
docs.text:
// Query all keys with a specific prefix
let results = storage.get_by_prefix(b"user:")?;

for (key, value) in results {
    println!("{:?} = {:?}", key, value);
}

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Transaction Monitor (bitvmx_transaction_monitor) is a real-time tracking system that connects to an Indexer and persistently tracks UTXOs and blocks, emitting status updates when transactions reach confirmation thresholds.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Real-Time Tracking: Continuous monitoring of UTXOs and transactions
  • Confirmation Thresholds: Configurable notification triggers
  • Persistent State: Maintains monitoring state across restarts
  • Event Notifications: Callback-based status updates

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-transaction-monitor = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitvmx_transaction_monitor::TransactionMonitor;

// Initialize monitor
let monitor = TransactionMonitor::new(config)?;

// Track a UTXO
monitor.track_utxo(outpoint, |status| {
    println!("UTXO status: {:?}", status);
})?;

// Track a transaction
monitor.track_tx(txid, 6, |confirmations| {
    println!("Confirmations: {}", confirmations);
})?;

docs.title: Monitoring UTXOs
docs.text:
// Monitor UTXO until spent
monitor.track_until_spent(outpoint, |spent_in| {
    println!("UTXO spent in tx: {}", spent_in);
})?;

// Check UTXO status
let status = monitor.get_utxo_status(outpoint)?;

docs.title: Transaction Confirmations
docs.text:
// Wait for specific confirmation count
monitor.wait_for_confirmations(txid, 6, |confirmations| {
    if confirmations >= 6 {
        println!("Transaction confirmed!");
    }
})?;

docs.title: RSK Pegin Monitoring
docs.text:
// Monitor RSK pegin transactions
monitor.monitor_rsk_pegin(address, |pegin_event| {
    println!("Pegin detected: {:?}", pegin_event);
})?;

docs.text:
High-level guide for using the BitVMX Wallet.

Detailed API Reference

For comprehensive API documentation with all types, functions, and modules, see the bitvmx_wallet Rust docs →

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BitVMX Wallet (bitvmx_wallet) provides wallet management for handling Bitcoin transactions and hierarchical key derivation.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• HD Wallet Support: BIP32/BIP44 hierarchical deterministic wallets
  • Transaction Building: Construct and sign Bitcoin transactions
  • Address Generation: Derive addresses from seeds
  • UTXO Management: Track and manage unspent outputs

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
bitvmx-wallet = { git = "https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git", branch = "main" }

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
use bitvmx_wallet::Wallet;

// Initialize wallet from seed
let wallet = Wallet::from_seed(seed_phrase)?;

// Generate a receiving address
let address = wallet.get_new_address()?;

// Get balance
let balance = wallet.get_balance()?;

docs.title: Transaction Creation
docs.text:
// Build a transaction
let tx = wallet.build_tx()
    .add_recipient(recipient_address, amount)?
    .with_fee_rate(fee_rate)?
    .build()?;

// Sign the transaction
let signed_tx = wallet.sign_tx(tx)?;

// Broadcast
wallet.broadcast(signed_tx)?;

docs.title: Key Derivation
docs.text:
// Derive keys using BIP44 path
let key = wallet.derive_key("m/44'/0'/0'/0/0")?;

// Get extended public key
let xpub = wallet.get_xpub()?;

docs.title: Union Bridge Technical Documentation
docs.text: Union Bridge is a trust-minimized bridge protocol for BTC transfers between Bitcoin and Rootstock, implemented using BitVMX's multi-party optimistic proving system.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
BitVMX Verification Layer - Multi-party optimistic proving system operating on Bitcoin - Fraud-proof verification mechanism - RISC-V virtual machine for computation verification - Hash chain commitments for state tracking

Bitcoin Layer - Taproot scripts for complex transaction logic - Time-locked contracts for challenge periods - Packet-based transaction batching - SPV (Simplified Payment Verification) proofs

Rootstock Layer - Bridge smart contracts for token minting/burning - Light client for Bitcoin header verification - Event emission system for cross-chain communication

Operator Network - Permissionless functionary participation - Collateral staking and slashing mechanisms - Event monitoring and relay services - Challenge submission system

docs.title: Packet-Based Architecture
docs.text:
Union Bridge uses a packet system that groups multiple bridge operations together:

  • Capital Efficiency: Security bonds are reused across operations within a packet
  • Cost Amortization: Bitcoin transaction fees spread across multiple transfers
  • Batched Processing: Multiple peg-outs handled in single Bitcoin transaction sequence

Benefits: - Reduces per-operation costs - Improves operator capital utilization - Increases system throughput

docs.title: Enabler System
docs.text:
The enabler manages functionary participation:

Registration: Operators stake collateral to participate in bridge operations

Penalty Enforcement: Slashing mechanism for malicious behavior

Reward Distribution: Honest operators receive fees for processing operations

Exit Mechanism: Time-locked withdrawal for operator collateral

docs.title: Stopwatch Timelock Optimization
docs.text:
Union Bridge implements an optimized time-lock mechanism:

  • Challenge period begins when assertion is made
  • Pauses during active disputes
  • Resumes after dispute resolution
  • Expires to release funds if no valid challenge

This balances security (adequate time for fraud detection) with efficiency (minimal delay for honest operations).

docs.title: 1-of-N Honest Assumption
docs.text:
Union Bridge operates under the assumption that at least one participant remains honest. This differs fundamentally from federated bridges requiring honest majorities.

Security Guarantee: The bridge remains secure if any single honest operator exists to challenge fraudulent operations.

Comparison with Alternatives:

Bridge Type Security Assumption Attack Threshold Federated (m-of-n multisig) Honest majority m+ colluding parties Committee-based ⅔+ honest ⅓+ colluding parties Union Bridge (1-of-n) Any one honest n-1 colluding parties

docs.title: Economic Security
docs.text:
Operators stake collateral that can be slashed for malicious behavior:

Attack Cost > Collateral at Risk + Opportunity Cost
Attack Profit = 0 (fraud is blocked)

Rational actors have no economic incentive to attempt fraud.

docs.title: Fraud Proof System
docs.text:
When fraudulent operations are detected:

  1. Honest operator submits challenge transaction
  2. BitVMX executes fraud proof on-chain
  3. Bitcoin Script verifies the proof deterministically
  4. Malicious operator's collateral is slashed
  5. Challenger receives reward from slashed funds

docs.title: Peg-In (Bitcoin → Rootstock)
docs.text:
Phase 1: Bitcoin Deposit 1. User sends BTC to Taproot peg-in address 2. Transaction confirms on Bitcoin (typically 6 confirmations) 3. SPV proof is constructed

Phase 2: Proof Relay 1. Operator monitors Bitcoin for deposits 2. Constructs inclusion proof with block header 3. Submits proof to Rootstock bridge contract

Phase 3: Token Minting 1. Bridge contract verifies SPV proof 2. Confirms Bitcoin finality 3. Mints wrapped BTC to user's Rootstock address

Security: Relies on Bitcoin's proof-of-work consensus. No trust in operators required—anyone can relay valid proofs.

docs.title: Peg-Out (Rootstock → Bitcoin)
docs.text:
Phase 1: Token Burning 1. User calls burn function on bridge contract 2. Contract records burn event with destination address 3. Event is emitted for operator monitoring

Phase 2: Packet Creation 1. Operator collects multiple burn events 2. Groups them into a packet for efficiency 3. Constructs Bitcoin transaction sequence

Phase 3: Bitcoin Submission 1. Kickoff transaction initiates the peg-out on Bitcoin 2. Operator locks collateral 3. Assert transaction claims validity of burns

Phase 4: Challenge Period - Duration: Configurable based on packet value (hours to days) - Purpose: Allow honest operators to detect and challenge fraud - Outcome: Proceed to unlock if no valid challenge

Phase 5: Finalization - If no challenge: Unlock transaction releases BTC to recipients - If challenged: Fraud proof executed, fraudulent packet rejected

Security: 1-of-n assumption guarantees at least one operator will challenge invalid packets.

docs.title: Light Client Framework
docs.text: Union Bridge implements a flexible light client system adaptable to different blockchain architectures:

docs.title: Bitcoin Light Client on Rootstock
docs.text:
• Verifies Bitcoin block headers
  • Validates proof-of-work
  • Confirms transaction inclusion via Merkle proofs
  • Tracks longest chain for finality

docs.title: Rootstock State Verification on Bitcoin
docs.text:
• Zero-knowledge proofs for block validation
  • Transaction existence proofs
  • State commitment verification
  • Event log inclusion proofs

docs.title: Adaptability
docs.text: The light client framework is designed to support various blockchain architectures beyond Rootstock, enabling Union Bridge to be deployed for other chains.

docs.title: Kickoff Transaction
docs.text:
Inputs: Operator's funding inputs
Outputs:
  - Connector output (spent by subsequent tx)
  - Challenge output (allows disputes)
  - Fee output

docs.title: Assert Transaction
docs.text:
Inputs: Kickoff connector output
Outputs:
  - Assertion commitment
  - Timelock output (challenge period)

docs.title: Challenge Transaction
docs.text:
Inputs: Challenge output from kickoff
Outputs:
  - Fraud proof data
  - Dispute resolution outputs

docs.title: Unlock Transaction
docs.text:
Inputs: Assert timelock output (after challenge period)
Outputs:
  - BTC to user addresses (from packet)
  - Operator collateral return

docs.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
docs.text:
Union Bridge uses ZK proofs for efficient verification:

Block Validity: Proves Rootstock blocks follow consensus rules

Transaction Inclusion: Proves specific transaction exists in block

State Transition: Proves contract state changes correctly

Event Emission: Proves event log entry exists

ZK proofs enable compact verification of complex computations on Bitcoin.

docs.title: Monitoring Peg-Ins
docs.text:
Operators monitor Bitcoin for deposits:

GET /bitcoin/blocks/latest
GET /bitcoin/tx/{txid}/confirmations
POST /rootstock/bridge/relay-proof

docs.title: Processing Peg-Outs
docs.text:
Operators monitor Rootstock for burns:

GET /rootstock/events?type=burn
GET /rootstock/bridge/pending-packets
POST /bitcoin/submit-packet

docs.title: Challenge Submission
docs.text:
Monitoring for fraud:

GET /bitcoin/packets/active
POST /bitcoin/challenge
POST /bitcoin/fraud-proof

For complete API specifications, see the API Reference section.

docs.title: Operator Requirements
docs.text:
Infrastructure: - Bitcoin full node (archival or pruned with relevant blocks) - Rootstock full node - Monitoring service for both chains - Key management for signing transactions

Collateral: - Sufficient BTC to cover packet value - Additional margin for Bitcoin fees - Staking period commitment

Network Connectivity: - Reliable connection to both networks - Low latency for timely challenge submission

docs.title: Gas Costs
docs.text:
Bitcoin: - Kickoff tx: ~500 vBytes - Assert tx: ~300 vBytes - Unlock tx: ~200 vBytes + user outputs - Challenge tx: Variable based on fraud proof complexity

Rootstock: - Proof relay: ~100k gas - Token minting: ~50k gas - Token burning: ~30k gas

docs.title: Challenge Period Configuration
docs.text:
Recommended challenge periods based on packet value:

Packet Value Challenge Period Security Reasoning < 1 BTC 12 hours Lower risk, faster finality 1-10 BTC 24 hours Balanced risk/speed 10-100 BTC 48 hours Higher risk, need detection time > 100 BTC 72+ hours Maximum security

docs.title: Testnet Deployment
docs.text:
Union Bridge is deployed on Bitcoin testnet and Rootstock testnet:

  • Test peg-in/peg-out flows
  • Simulate challenge scenarios
  • Measure gas costs and timing
  • Verify fraud proof execution

docs.title: Mainnet Deployment
docs.text:
Production deployment on Bitcoin mainnet and Rootstock mainnet includes:

  • Multi-sig governance for upgrades (temporary, transitioning to immutability)
  • Monitored operator set
  • Graduated value limits during initial phase
  • Circuit breakers for anomalous activity

docs.text:

  • Case Study: Production implementation details
  • BitVMX Core Concepts: Underlying verification system
  • Protocol Builder API: Building bridge protocols

docs.title: Getting Started with BitVMX
docs.text: Welcome to BitVMX! This guide will help you get up and running with the BitVMX platform.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BitVMX is a platform for disputable computation on Bitcoin. Before diving in, you'll need to:

  1. Understand the prerequisites
  2. Install the required tools
  3. Set up your development environment
  4. Run your first example

docs.title: Quick Navigation
docs.text:
• Prerequisites

    Check system requirements and dependencies needed for BitVMX development.

    Prerequisites

  • Installation

    Step-by-step installation guide for BitVMX and all components.

    Installation

  • Quick Start

    Get up and running in minutes with our quick start tutorial.

    Quick Start

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
By the end of this section, you will:

  • Have BitVMX installed and configured
  • Understand the basic architecture
  • Run your first BitVMX example
  • Know where to go next for deeper learning

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Once you've completed the getting started guide:

  • Explore Core Concepts to understand how BitVMX works
  • Check out Tutorials for hands-on examples
  • Read the Developer Guide for building your own protocols

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This guide walks you through installing BitVMX and its components.

docs.title: BitVMX Workspace
docs.text: The recommended way to work with BitVMX is using the workspace that includes all components.

docs.title: Clone the Workspace
docs.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-workspace.git
cd rust-bitvmx-workspace

If you already cloned without submodules:

git submodule init
git submodule update --remote --checkout

docs.title: Build the Workspace
docs.text:
cargo build --release

This will build all components. The initial build may take 15-30 minutes depending on your system.

docs.title: Individual Components
docs.text: You can also install individual components:

docs.title: BitVMX Client
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/FairgateLabs/rust-bitvmx-client.git
cd rust-bitvmx-client
cargo build --release

docs.title: BitVMX CPU
docs.text:
cd BitVMX-CPU
cargo build --release

docs.title: Docker Installation
docs.text:
For a containerized environment:

git clone https://github.com/FairgateLabs/docker-bitvmx.git
cd docker-bitvmx
docker-compose up -d

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Test that BitVMX is working:

cargo test --release

Run a simple example:

cargo run --release --example hello

docs.title: Build Errors
docs.text:
If you encounter build errors:

  1. Ensure Rust is up to date: rustup update
  2. Clean and rebuild: cargo clean && cargo build --release
  3. Check Troubleshooting Guide

docs.title: Dependency Issues
docs.text:
Install missing system dependencies:

Ubuntu/DebianmacOS 
sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev

brew install openssl pkg-config

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Now that BitVMX is installed, proceed to the Quick Start guide.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before installing BitVMX, ensure your system meets the following requirements.

docs.title: Operating System
docs.text:
BitVMX is developed and tested on:

  • Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+, Arch Linux, Fedora) - Recommended
  • macOS (10.15+)
  • Windows (via WSL2)

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Minimum requirements:

  • CPU: x86_64 or ARM64
  • RAM: 8GB minimum, 16GB+ recommended
  • Storage: 20GB+ free space
  • Network: Internet connection for downloading dependencies

docs.title: Rust Toolchain
docs.text:
BitVMX is written in Rust. Install the latest stable Rust:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Verify installation:

rustc --version
cargo --version

docs.title: Git
docs.text:
Install Git for version control:

Ubuntu/DebianmacOSArch Linux 
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git

brew install git

sudo pacman -S git

docs.title: Bitcoin Core (Optional)
docs.text:
For testing and development with regtest/testnet:

  • Download from bitcoin.org
  • Or use Docker: docker pull bitcoin/bitcoin

docs.title: Docker (Optional)
docs.text:
Recommended for running RISC-V compilation and testing:

  • Install from docker.com

docs.title: Python 3.8+
docs.text:
For testing scripts and utilities:

python3 --version

docs.title: Node.js (for Union Bridge Smart Contracts)
docs.text:
If working with Union Bridge:

curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_18.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt install -y nodejs

docs.title: Verify Prerequisites
docs.text:
Run this checklist before proceeding:

  • Rust toolchain installed (rustc --version)
  • Git installed (git --version)
  • Sufficient disk space (20GB+)
  • Internet connection available

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Once all prerequisites are met, proceed to Installation.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get started with BitVMX in minutes! This guide will walk you through running your first BitVMX example.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Ensure you have completed the Installation guide.

docs.title: Running Your First Example
docs.text: BitVMX includes several examples to help you get started. Let's run the Union Bridge committee setup example.

docs.title: 1. Start a Bitcoin Node
docs.text:
First, start a local Bitcoin regtest node:

cargo run --release --example union setup_bitcoin_node

This starts a Bitcoin node in regtest mode for testing.

docs.title: 2. Start BitVMX Instance
docs.text:
In a new terminal, start a BitVMX instance with default operators:

cargo run --release all

Or start fresh (clearing previous data):

rm -rf /tmp/regtest/
cargo run --release all --fresh

docs.title: 3. Run the Committee Flow
docs.text:
In another terminal, run the committee setup:

cargo run --release --example union committee

This will:

  1. Create a committee of operators
  2. Generate aggregated keys
  3. Set up the protocol structure
  4. Display the committee information

docs.title: What Just Happened?
docs.text:
You just:

  • ✅ Started a local Bitcoin network
  • ✅ Launched BitVMX operators
  • ✅ Created a multi-party committee
  • ✅ Generated cryptographic keys using MuSig2

docs.title: Explore More Examples
docs.text:
Try other Union Bridge examples:

# Request a peg-in
cargo run --release --example union request_pegin

# Accept a peg-in
cargo run --release --example union accept_pegin

# Test advance funds
cargo run --release --example union advance_funds

docs.title: Learn Core Concepts
docs.text:
Now that you've seen BitVMX in action, learn how it works:

  • Architecture Overview
  • Challenge-Response Protocol
  • Union Bridge Introduction

docs.title: Build Your Own
docs.text:
Ready to build? Check out:

  • Your First Protocol Tutorial
  • Developer Guide
  • API Reference

docs.title: Port Already in Use
docs.text:
If you see "address already in use" errors:

# Kill existing processes
pkill -f bitvmx-client
pkill -f bitcoind

docs.title: Connection Errors
docs.text:
Ensure all services are running:

# Check Bitcoin node
bitcoin-cli -regtest getblockchaininfo

# Check BitVMX services
ps aux | grep bitvmx

For more help, see the Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Union Bridge
docs.text:
Technical Documentation

Looking for a detailed specification of the Union Bridge? See Union Bridge.

The Union Bridge is a trust-minimized bridge protocol designed to enable the secure and efficient transfer of BTC between the Bitcoin network and Rootstock. Rootstock is the longest running and leading Bitcoin sidechain, and the bridge is key to extending Bitcoin's functionality and promoting interoperability.

docs.title: Core Motivation and Security Breakthrough
docs.text:
The need for Union stems from the limitations of traditional bridging solutions, which often rely on trusted intermediaries or complex multi-signature schemes. These methods introduce significant centralization risks or prove economically inefficient, compromising Bitcoin's inherent trustless nature.

The Union protocol is built to solve this by leveraging BitVMX, an optimistic proving system that allows for the verification of computations on Bitcoin. This technology enforces correct peg-out validation using fraud proofs.

The fundamental security breakthrough of Union lies in its trust model: it operates securely under the assumption that at least one participant remains honest (a 1-of-N honest approach). This approach stands in stark contrast to conventional federated systems, which require an honest majority (T-of-N). This design choice enhances decentralization and results in a fully non-custodial and permissionless bridge mechanism that upholds Bitcoin's core principles.

docs.title: Bridge Operation (Peg-in and Peg-out)
docs.text:
The Union Bridge is a two-way peg system connecting Bitcoin (Bs) and Rootstock (Bt). The process involves:

• Peg-in: Users transfer BTC from Bitcoin to Rootstock. They lock their BTC funds on Bitcoin and receive an equivalent wrapped asset (RBTC) on Rootstock.

• Peg-out: Users transfer wrapped BTC from Rootstock back to Bitcoin. Any functionary can act as an operator to advance the BTC to the user and then recover these funds by proving the validity of the peg-out operation on Rootstock.

The protocol prioritizes speed, particularly in the most common case where all committee members agree to sign the transfer. If there is a dispute or non-cooperation, an operator advances the funds and uses the BitVMX dispute system to be reimbursed later. The expectation is that disputes will be rare because the system is designed such that rational actors follow the protocol.

docs.title: Key Architectural Innovations
docs.text:
The protocol introduces several mechanisms to ensure scalability, security, and capital efficiency:

  1. Capital Efficiency through Packets: The packet-based architecture groups multiple bridge operations (VMXOs) together so they can share and reuse security deposits. This means the required capital grows sub-linearly with the value locked, significantly improving efficiency.

  2. Functionary Management via Enablers: An innovative enabler system manages the participation of functionaries (the entities operating the bridge) and enforces penalties. Enablers act as participation tokens; if a functionary misbehaves or loses a dispute, their remaining enablers are "burnt," preventing them from participating in future operations for that packet and allowing their security deposit to be slashed.

  3. Flexible Validation: The protocol utilizes a flexible light client framework that allows for cross-chain validation and can be adapted to various blockchain architectures and consensus mechanisms.

  4. Optimized Time Management: An efficient stop watch mechanism is included to optimize time-lock management in the multi-step verification processes, making the dispute resolution phases more efficient than sequential time-locks.

In summary, the Union Bridge is designed as a practical and scalable solution for Bitcoin interoperability that maintains strong security guarantees, minimizes trust assumptions, and enhances efficiency compared to existing federated systems.

docs.text:

  • Union: A Trust-minimized Bridge for Rootstock
